body.text: The Cockroach movement in India and the “cost of living” crisis in Europe that resulted in protests across France and Germany in recent weeks are not just an expression of discontentment fuelled by localised issues but symbols of a broader crisis of global capitalism.

According to William I. Robinson, social critic and professor of sociology at University of California, Santa Barbara, one of the dimensions of this crisis—social reproduction—seems to have played a role in catalysing these movements from below through an explosion of “critical consciousness” and “social solidarity”. This is despite the sustained attempts to divide the working classes through the use of propaganda, threats, and mass psychology by agents of what he terms “the transnational elite”.

He says that while these protests attempt to resist capitalism’s bid to further enhance the power of the “transnational elite” at the common man’s expense, the system’s own trajectory, felt through intensified intra-capitalist competition and class wars, has been undermining its capacity to reproduce itself and is therefore leading us to a point of no return.

The rise of AI could be seen in this context as a technological breakthrough that further intensifies this crisis. The transition from precariatisation of labour, involving the shift towards unprotected employment, to the elimination of labour could, at least in theory, end capital-labour relations altogether and, therefore, capitalism as we have known it all along. The wars, chaos, and repression, then, become new sources of super-profits and accumulation in this systemic collapse.

Prof. Robinson’s latest book, Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class, explores the emergence of the new “lords of the world” in the age of AI, and how they are reshaping the world around us to consolidate power. In this interview, he talks about the rise of AI, technofeudalism, the societal role played by the far right, the new forms of class struggle, and more. Edited excerpts:

AI, much like the extraction of fossil fuels, represents an ability to concentrate disparate sources of value, bring them under centralised control, and extract rent. Do you agree with this assessment? If so, does it not represent a particularly chilling dynamic in the way capital has accumulated over the years and continues to do so today?

Yes. What you’re raising is extremely important and goes to the heart of what’s going on in the global capitalist economy at this time, and you’re right that the story of what is going on with AI is actually something intrinsic to capitalist development and capital accumulation to begin with.

Harry Braverman [in his book, Labour & Monopoly Capital] building up on [Karl] Marx, laid out how capital seeks to deskill labour, to cheapen labour, to take control of the labour process away from labour and give it to capital. That’s been going on for decades; actually, it’s been going on for centuries. We know that, and Marx already analysed that. But what AI does is that first, it turbocharges that process, and second, it threatens to not just deskill and precariatise labour but to actually eliminate labour.
Moving forward, capital’s drive to maximise profits through AI is going to undermine the ability of capitalism to reproduce itself, of capital to reproduce itself, and that’s the crisis.

Something else is [also] going on with AI. It is heightening intra-capitalist competition and also shifting the sectors of capital that are hegemonic. The tech sector is able to extract not just surplus value from labour but [also] rents from other sectors of capital that actually do the exploitation. That has a whole lot of implications for intra-capitalist competition and dynamics globally.

Moreover, AI is extremely expensive. The construction of data centres requires hundreds of billions dollars in investment. It means that constant capital is enormously growing relative to variable capital, or that fixed capital is enormously expanding relative to workers, to living labour, which is variable capital. And so, this contradiction and the decline in the rate of profit in the long run is something of a new territory.

AI capital is constructing AI in order to expand profits and continue to accumulate, and also in order to control global labour. And it’s going to backfire on capital in the long run and intensify all of these contradictions at a pace we can’t imagine.

The newest and the most important source of profits worldwide now and the whole strategy of accumulation being put forward by this new hegemonic block of capital is repression, warfare, genocide, conflict and chaos. And so, we are also moving towards World War III. We are moving towards a dystopic future nightmare society that previously existed only in Hollywood films.

The idea of technofeudalism has resonated with many of us, and you have rightly argued in your book that the system is still driven by the law of value and capital’s need for expanded accumulation. How useful is the feudal analogy in understanding the nature of power and the loss of freedom in today’s world?

At the level of description, it’s useful to talk about technofeudalism and how we are increasingly reverting to a feudalist system. But it’s not at the level of analysis, theory, or the explanatory level. It’s just a description that this is what it looks like.

Let me first say that Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism [by the economist Yanis Varoufakis] is really brilliant. I understand why he is using that term. The problem, though, is that it’s not feudalism; it’s very distinct from feudalism.

Varoufakis explains how the circulation of surplus value is taking new directions than it was previously taking, thanks to digitalisation and AI. But rents are not new to capitalism. They were always there. The idea here is that an enormous amount of profit is going to a core group of capitalists bound up with AI, with technology corporations, and also with the military-industrial complex.

Historically, Marx analysed that. At a certain moment, there are super-profits. Where do the super-profits come from? It’s not that they are exploiting their workers more than other sectors are exploiting their workers. It’s that profit made in different sectors migrates over to the super-profits sector.
Massive amounts of capital are needed to get those super-profits or to get those rents from other sectors of capital. And that’s what’s going on right now.

With globalisation, you have the unleashing of an unprecedented historical centralisation and concentration of capital on a world scale in transnational capital, in this transnational capitalist class. We’ve never seen such centralisation in transnational capital and that brings tremendous political influence, structural power, and ideological and cultural power, especially through the new technologies. These people do appear as lords of the world because they are the lords of the world, but they are capitalist lords of the world, not feudal lords of the world.

The importance of historical figures [such as Modi and Trump] is that they are generating and pushing forward the political, social, and cultural conditions which deflect from the epochal crisis of global capitalism, and which disorganise and atomise, divide, and confuse the labouring masses. So they are absolutely crucial figures to undermine the ability of the labouring masses to challenge the domination of this unprecedented transnational capitalist class, and the elites that go together with the transnational capitalist class.

The fascist project allows capital to accumulate. It gives everything it needs for accumulation, including repression of the working class to accumulate. In turn, capital turns to supporting the political project of fascism.

What’s so dangerous here in the US is that this hegemonic block of AI capital brings together the triangulation of tech capital with military-industry repression capital and with transnational finance capital (sic). They are all linked to the new ruling class here and worldwide. Now that block of capital decided over the last 4-5 years that it is going to link up with fascism in the state: with Trumpism, with Modiism, with Javier Milei in Argentina, and with Netanyahu in Israel.

I would like to depart from the lens through which you have examined the AI age and consider a psychosocial dimension. Will the development of critical consciousness among ordinary people eventually produce a powerful resistance to oligarchic control even in the absence of Marxist ideals?

Of course. Masses of people don’t need to read Capital and say they are Marxists to understand what’s going on. All over the world, people are in rebellion without saying they are Marxists or without necessarily having read anything that Marx wrote.

The psychological development is extremely central to all of this, but it doesn’t just come from one individual. The ruling class is using a lot of psychological warfare against us. And that psychological warfare is waged at every level. Unfortunately, AI allows them to wage a new age warfare, through social media, the attention economy, and now even through intervention in electoral processes.

Capital has fragmented us, atomised us, and turned us against one another. So as part of our mass struggles, we need to think of ways to recompose the global working class. We don’t need Marx to do that. What we need are new ways to get together and realise that we are facing the same conditions, and therefore we have the same struggle, and that is what we are seeing all over: with the Cockroach movement in India, with the students right now in France.
Another [challenge] is a crisis of social reproduction, of social disintegration everywhere, how communities are collapsing. It’s taking place in India, here in the US, in Africa.

Everywhere we look, there’s mass social disintegration, social decomposition, and collapse and social crisis. Billions of people can’t survive; they can’t reproduce themselves and their communities, so a part of our struggle is the struggle for social reproduction. And increasingly, that’s a vector of emerging class consciousness, or collective consciousness.
We need that independent thought, that critical consciousness, and the more we push forward in our struggle, the more that counter-consciousness to the fascist consciousness expands.

I also want to point out why the students’ rebellion in France is actually a working-class struggle against AI and a restructuring of global capitalism driven by digitalisation and the epochal crisis of global capitalism.

The more global capital does not need workers, the more workers become surplus humanity, surplus labour. The more AI, machinery, and constant capital takes over, the less transnational capital needs young people that are trained to read and to be able to think about things a little bit in the abstract.
You don’t need to give education to people who just become surplus labour, surplus humanity. You just need to control them and even genocide them, or lock them up in mass incarceration.

Why is education being savagely defunded in France while there are all these trillions of dollars for wars and other things and for investment, speculative investment, and AI? Because capital no longer needs the social reproduction of the great centres of the global working class.

And so you cut education, health, any lifeline to social reproduction because capital does not need your social reproduction if you are surplus. That’s crucial; that’s why students going on to have strikes to demand a bigger educational budget is at the heart of global class struggle pushing against global capital and the new ruling class.

In your book, you write: “The violent upheavals and civil wars that will come—that are already upon us—will be as much intra-elite as class wars.” Could these intra-elite struggles increasingly take the form of geopolitical and civilisational conflict? Do you think such a dynamic could lead to a new Cold War or even a major military confrontation between competing blocs?

Absolutely, we are moving to a situation of escalating geopolitical conflict. There are geo-economic and geopolitical blocks that are emerging and they are merging consciously because the agents that have built these blocks are pushing them.

Trump is trying to build a Western Hemisphere block with the Monroe Doctrine and his corollary, the Donroe Doctrine, the shield of the Americas and the escalating military intervention of the US and the political intervention to make them extreme right neo-fascist block of power in the whole western hemisphere.
China is trying to consolidate its position of the Chinese state and the ruling class, consolidating a Sino-centric Asian economy and expanding outward from there.

[But] we don’t want to conflate transnational capital with the state. They are connected [and] they do form a contradictory unit. You can’t talk about capital outside of the state. You can’t talk about the capitalist state outside of capital. But analytically, we first have to separate it out.

What does this capitalist state have to do with China, the US, India, Colombia, wherever it is? The capitalist state has to reproduce capital inside its territory, and it has to give everything that capital needs to accumulate.

What does that mean? It means creating a stable macroeconomic environment and keeping your finances in order. It means controlling the working class and trying to break unions, and with their strikes, replace the striking workers. It means lowering environmental regulations so capital will come to your country rather than go somewhere else. It means changing the tax structure so capitalists are taxed less and workers are taxed more. We have the situation right now in the US.
You must reproduce and expand capital inside your nation-state, but the second mandate that the capitalist state has is to achieve legitimacy and hold together the social order internally.

The capitalist state needs to legitimise itself, and it needs to reproduce and hold together the social order; those two mandates are contradictory. One nullifies the other; the more you generate the conditions to please capital and have it come to your territory, the more you cannot [ensure] internal cohesion of the social order and reproduction of the working class people. So, that is a contradiction, and that contradiction is part of the story of geopolitical confrontation.
It is not that capital operating in the US is fighting with capital operating in India or in China and each go to their governments and say: “Please go to war just for us.”

That’s not the situation. In the 21st century, what capital wants is to be able to move all over the world in this age of globalisation without any impediments. It doesn’t want borders to get in its way.

The Chinese state very tightly controls Chinese private capital, more than the US state controls capital operating in the US. And so there’s all this mounting state competition, and mounting geopolitical tensions.

We are moving to an escalating geopolitical conflict that in fact could end up in World War III. Capital just wants an open global economy to exploit whatever you possibly can; control wherever you can. States superimpose themselves on that, and bring about a geopolitical and geo-economic restructuring. That’s coming from the capitalist state, not from the transnational capitalist class.

The concentration of wealth has coincided with a reluctance among governments to generate aggregate demand through fiscal expansion or greater taxation of the wealthy. In such a scenario, do you think the contradictions of capitalism could generate a sufficiently powerful popular movement to demand the redistribution of wealth?

We at the nation-state level struggle and demand that our states intervene, tax capital, and use that taxation of capital to capture the surplus being used in the capitalist circuit through social spending, etc.

There is this structural power of transnational capital to undermine redistribution downward. It wants states to not do that. But there’s also the question that we discussed earlier: its leading edge of accumulation is the global police state.

The government doesn’t tell us that it’s expanding the military budget because that is where transnational capital accumulates, and it’s cutting the education budget because you don’t need to reproduce that labour.

The more we understand what’s going on, the more the masses of people are better equipped to develop the strategies of resistance. Not only can we but we’re doing that in every corner of the world all the time.

Capitalism’s drive for accumulation appears fundamentally at odds with the ecological limits of the planet. How do you see the ecological crisis reshaping the struggle between capital and labour in the coming decades?

The crisis of the planetary ecosystem is much more than just climate change. This is absolutely central to everything that’s going on in the world in ways that are not necessarily apparent to our eyes. Global capitalism is facing an epochal crisis in which the conditions that make possible the reproduction of global capital are increasingly being undermined. And above all, you cannot reproduce capital in the face of ecological collapse.

You’re going to have the situation where agriculture collapses. At least, industrial, digitalised, large-scale, corporate agriculture. It will collapse, and that will lead to food shortages, and that will have a cascading effect on the uprising of people with food riots. It will also have an effect in which millions of people whose labour are not needed will just be sealed off by a global police state that abandons them and then they die of hunger.
Military spending is rising across much of the world. How do you interpret this trend in the context of the arguments you make in your book?

Military wars and military expenditure are rooted in the ecological crisis. When there are prolonged droughts in certain countries, hunger starts and movement of people starts, and world wars come in and take advantage of that. Some of the conflicts in West Africa have very significant ecological dimensions.

All of that is deeply connected. Capital cannot reproduce itself in the face of a planetary ecosystem. The blind impulse to endlessly accumulate makes it impossible for capital to resolve the ecological crisis. Maybe its organic intellectuals will try to hasten a green transition. But the green transition under the capitalist relations of production is also very contradictory because the idea is: if you’re going to have green transition through capitalism, you have to guarantee alternative sources of energy and the resources needed for that energy are themselves profitable, because the accumulation of capital has to be profit.

Just to give you an example, here in the US we have national parks and now they are being privatised so portions of national parks can have mining operations that AI needs, that green technology needs.

Green capitalism is a contradiction in terms. But I want to go back also to even genocides. What does it mean for the global working class for our struggle from below? The system does not need our social reproduction.
It can even turn genociding us and controlling us into profit; we have to think about how, at the local level, we ensure our social reproduction, our collective community social reproduction.

Finally, we need to understand that the concept of the global police state is much greater than police in the streets repressing protestors. The global police state [also] opens up space for accumulation. The act of warfare, the act of genocide themselves are enormously profitable. Expanding military expenditure, private expenditure, all organised around the global police state is the new face of global accumulation.
Abhishek Mukherjee is an independent journalist based in Kolkata.
